Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

An analytic functional has a compact real carrier. A local generalized function should not need a preferred compact carrier or a chosen boundary. We obtain such objects by ignoring the part of a representative supported on the boundary of an open set. Carrier splitting makes restriction possible; completeness modulo smaller carriers makes countably many compatible pieces fit together. The resulting objects can extend across a boundary even when no distributional extension exists.

All vector spaces are over , and pairings are complex linear. Euclidean dimensions are positive. For a real compact , has the meaning proved in Analytic tests and real carriers, with its germ action in Theorem 5 and support-preserving distribution inclusion in Theorem 6. We write for the smallest real carrier from Recovering analytic data from harmonic fields, Theorem 6. The two principal inputs are the full finite splitting and completeness theorems in Localizing analytic sources without analytic cutoffs, Theorems 2 and 6.

Existing distribution restriction and gluing are proved in Local data and compatible products, Theorems 1.1–2.1. The finite-order bound on each compact set is (1.2) in Order, positivity and distributional limits, whose test-topology argument proves its equivalence with continuity. Cutoffs, compactness, scalar calculus and the elementary exponential estimates used here are in metric foundations, Sections 12–13, and integration foundations, Sections 15–16. None of the constructions below uses a smooth partition to multiply an arbitrary hyperfunction.

For any open , define a section of to be a family The operations are componentwise. If is bounded, the -component determines the family, and the earlier restriction maps give the inverse correspondence. Thus (L1) agrees with (Q1).

Theorem 3 (the full local structure). These spaces have restriction to every open subset and unique gluing over every open cover. The support of is the complement of the union of open sets where it is zero. It is relatively closed, satisfies the support identity (Q5), and vanishes on the complement of its support.

Proof. Restriction in (L1) forgets components not contained in the smaller open set. For compatible sections on an arbitrary cover , fix a bounded open . The bounded opens cover , and the supplied components agree on overlaps. Theorem 2 gives one . For , the restriction of and the constructed agree on the cover ; uniqueness in Theorem 2 makes them equal. Therefore they form a family (L1). The same bounded-component argument proves both its required restrictions and uniqueness.

The union of zero neighborhoods is itself a zero region by this gluing uniqueness, so its complement has the claimed support property. For a bounded , a point of has a zero neighborhood for the family exactly when it has one for . The bounded support formula therefore gives . Applying this locally proves the assertion for arbitrary restrictions.

This restriction-and-gluing structure is what is meant by a sheaf here. No additional sheaf theorem is being used.

Distributions inside the local theory

Proposition 5 (faithful inclusion and regular loci). There are compatible linear injections for all Euclidean open sets, preserving support and agreeing with the analytic-functional inclusion for compact distributions. A hyperfunction is called smooth, or real analytic, on an open set when it is the image of a function of that class. The complements of these regular loci define relatively closed smooth and analytic singular supports.

Proof. Cover by relatively compact open sets with . Choose equal to one near . Extend the compact distribution to , use its analytic-functional inclusion, and take . This notation uses that proved inclusion before applying .

For two choices on overlapping patches, the difference of the compact distributions is zero on the overlap. Its analytic-functional support is exactly its distributional support, by Theorem 6 of the analytic-functional lesson. Formula (L2) therefore makes the difference of the local sections zero there. Theorem 3 glues them uniquely. The same argument proves independence of the cover, linearity, compatibility with restriction and agreement for an originally compact distribution.

Locally near , and its two notions of support agree. Formula (L2) consequently proves . This gives global support equality. If , every local restriction of is zero, so the existing distribution gluing theorem gives .

If local smooth functions represent the same hyperfunction, injectivity makes their distributions equal, and then the functions agree pointwise. The last assertion follows from the elementary bump test: a nonzero continuous value has, after a constant complex phase, positive real part on a small neighborhood and pairs positively with a nonnegative bump there. Thus the local functions glue uniquely. Smoothness and analyticity are local properties, so their regular sets are open. Their complements are relatively closed and lie in the ordinary support. Real analytic functions are smooth; hence smooth singular support is contained in analytic singular support.

The quotient in (Q1) would give a smaller space if analytic functionals were replaced by compact distributions. Exercise 2 gives an explicit obstruction to that replacement.

Operations on actual neighborhoods

Theorem 6 (local operations and analytic coordinate changes). The following operations are well defined and commute with restriction:

  1. Differentiation and multiplication by real analytic functions on , with the ordinary Leibniz rule. They do not enlarge support.
  2. Tensor products , with support contained in the product of supports, associativity, and the usual separate-variable derivative identities.
  3. For a real analytic diffeomorphism , a bijection with .

These operations agree with the existing distribution operations on their distributional inputs. The pullback assertion here concerns analytic diffeomorphisms.

Proof: derivatives and products. On a bounded patch with closure inside , choose a representative whose real compact carrier lies inside . Such representatives exist by taking the section on a slightly larger bounded open set with closure in . Apply the derivative or analytic-germ multiplication from Proposition 7 of the analytic-functional lesson, then take its local class.

If two representatives give the same section on a smaller open set, their difference is supported outside that set. Differentiation and analytic multiplication preserve its carrier, so the outputs still agree there. The local definitions therefore glue and commute with restriction. The analytic-functional Leibniz identity gives the multi-index formula follows by induction from the first derivative rule and Pascal's identity. Locality proves the support bounds. Finite sums give every differential operator with analytic coefficients.

Proof: tensor products. Choose such compact representatives on patches , , and use on . Replacing them by changes this by The first term has carrier disjoint from because its first factor is supported off ; the second has the analogous property in the second factor. The product-carrier bound is the one fully proved for analytic functionals. Thus all local choices agree, and rectangular patches plus Theorem 3 give a tensor product on the whole product open set. The same reasoning gives its support inclusion and restriction compatibility. Associativity and derivative identities hold on compact representatives by their iterated germ pairings, hence hold after gluing. For compact distributions those pairings agree with the distribution tensor; local cutoffs and injectivity prove agreement for general distributional inputs.

Coordinates on a real analytic manifold

Let be a Hausdorff second-countable real analytic manifold. For an analytic atlas , put . Define a section to be a family obeying the transition rule where both sections are first restricted to the relevant overlap.

Theorem 7 (independence of coordinates). Formula (M1) defines spaces independent of the analytic atlas, with restriction, arbitrary-cover gluing and support. It extends the Euclidean definition. Distribution inclusion, multiplication by analytic germs near the support and tensor products descend to these spaces.

Proof. On a triple overlap, the actual coordinate transitions compose. Theorem 6's composition law therefore gives exactly the cocycle identity needed in (M1). Now take any additional analytic chart . On the opens , transport by . The cocycle and (M1) make these local sections agree. Euclidean gluing supplies a unique section on .

Apply this construction to every chart of a second atlas. The resulting sections satisfy its transition rule, again by the cocycle on the common local intersections and uniqueness. Transporting back recovers the original section on each original chart, since equality holds on its cover by the new chart intersections. These constructions are inverse and agree on a common refinement, giving canonical atlas independence. At no point must a transition extend across the closure of its overlap: Theorem 6 defines its pullback on the actual open overlap using smaller compact representatives.

Restriction uses the restricted charts. Compatible sections on an arbitrary open cover glue in each chart by the Euclidean theorem, and the transition identities hold because they hold on a covering family of overlaps. This proves both global existence and uniqueness. The zero neighborhoods and their complement define support, and its coordinate transformation is (O1). For a Euclidean open set the identity chart and the same construction recover exactly (L1).

The existing scalar distribution coordinate convention has the same inverse absolute Jacobian as (O4). The local injective inclusions therefore respect (M1) and give a support-preserving inclusion of distributions on . Analytic multiplication respects coordinates because , as follows directly from (O4) on compact representatives and locality. Tensor products respect product charts: the inverse Jacobian of a product map is the product of the two inverse Jacobians, and the iterated analytic-functional pairing then gives the two separate pullbacks. The same gluing proves their intrinsic definition on products of manifolds.

Smooth and analytic regular loci on a manifold are defined in coordinates as above. Scalar functions transform by composition, so these loci and their singular supports are independent of the atlas.

Extension with the boundary retained

Theorem 8 (extension and all its ambiguity). If is open, every extends to with Consequently restriction has the exact sequences Thus all extensions satisfying (F2) form one coset of the boundary-supported space. No preferred extension is specified.

Proof: one bounded coordinate patch. For bounded Euclidean opens , a representative of a section on also belongs to . Its class on restricts to the original section and has support contained in . Thus every restriction from a bounded coordinate patch onto an open subset of that patch is onto. The subset is bounded too, so its representative is supplied by (Q1). Transport by the chart gives the same assertion on .

Proof: preserve the required zeros while extending. First glue the original on with zero on . These disjoint opens define a section on Choose countably many coordinate patches covering , each with bounded coordinate image. Such a cover exists: shrink every chart around every point to a coordinate ball with compact closure in its original image, then use second countability to select a countable subcover. The selection follows by the same basis argument used in Theorem 2, now with a countable manifold base.

Inductively suppose is defined on . Its restriction to extends to a section on by the one-patch result. Glue the two agreeing sections on These sections agree under every earlier restriction. Their increasing open domains cover , so Theorem 7 glues them to . The initial values on and on have never changed. This proves both extension and the support bound (F2). Empty sets and are included by taking the zero or identity construction as appropriate.

The kernel of restriction consists precisely of sections supported off , by the support characterization. This proves the first sequence in (F3), including surjectivity. Within the closure-supported space the kernel is supported in , proving the second. Subtracting two extensions and adding any such kernel element gives exactly the asserted coset.

The surjectivity of all restriction maps is called flabbiness. The proof retains the boundary in (F2). Replacing the closure by itself would generally be false.

Exercises with full solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — what an endpoint forgets. On , take a representative , where , possibly of infinite order. Find its support in , its restriction to , and its restriction to .

Solution. Both are carried by , so the class equals and its support is . On the remaining atom lies on the boundary, so its class is zero. On the atom lies inside, so the class is its nonzero interior point functional. This follows either from (Q5) or directly from the quotient and (L2).

Exercise 2 (advanced) — an extension beyond distributions. Regard on as a distribution and then as a hyperfunction. Prove that it has no distributional extension to any neighborhood of , while it has a hyperfunction extension to supported in .

Solution. If a distribution extended it near , finite order on a fixed compact neighborhood of that interval would give for tests supported there. Choose a nonnegative nonzero and set , . These supports lie in , and The exponential exceeds every inverse power: its power series contains a positive term of any prescribed degree. Taking degree greater than contradicts the finite-order bound. Theorem 8 supplies the hyperfunction extension with support in . Proposition 4 identifies it with an analytic functional carried there, but the contradiction shows it cannot be a distribution. Its existence is not an assertion that the divergent integral defines that functional.

Solution. The inverse is , with absolute derivative . Formula (O4) and the sign in a distributional derivative give The series converges by the point-moment estimate, or by the already proved germ pullback. In particular , and then . Since , its direct inverse absolute derivative is , giving the same result. Dropping the absolute Jacobian would change the scalar-function convention.

Exercise 7 (advanced) — a tensor which is still not a distribution. Let be the infinite point functional in Exercise 5 and . Describe , its support, and why it is not a distribution.

Solution. Its action on a holomorphic germ near is It is carried by and is nonzero on the constant germ, so (L2) gives exactly that support. If it were a compact distribution, its pushforward under the projection would be a compact distribution. Pairing with tests depending on shows that this pushforward has analytic functional . The exact compact-distribution inclusion and the proved non-distributional nature of give a contradiction. The compact pushforward is well defined by inserting a cutoff near the compact support, as in the earlier compact pairing theorem.

Exercise 8 (intermediate) — when the extension is unique. Show that if is both open and closed in , the extension in Theorem 8 with support in is unique. Explain the boundary ambiguity when is not closed.

Solution. For an open-and-closed , its relative boundary is empty, so the second kernel in (F3) is zero. Gluing the section with zero on the complementary open set gives the unique extension. In general (F3) says exactly that two closure-supported extensions differ by a section supported on . At any boundary point a nonzero point-supported section exists: take a point functional in a coordinate chart and glue its section with zero off that point; the two pieces agree away from it. Thus a nonempty boundary admits nonzero ambiguities. This is why extension across a boundary is an existence assertion, not a canonical zero-extension rule.
